extracted.intended_audience: regulated entities and stakeholders (EGU owners/operators, pipeline developers, state and Federal permitting agencies, and public commenters on the EPA rule)
extracted.subtask_short: EPA CCS pipeline and sequestration assessment
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of the EPA's evaluative criteria and standards used in the preamble to determine whether CO2 transport (pipelines) and geologic sequestration are "adequately demonstrated" for affected EGUs, including permitting, safety, siting, and timing considerations. Focuses on legal/regulatory requirements (NEPA, PHMSA, UIC Class VI), technical demonstrations, and proxies used in EPA modeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEPA compliance and level of review
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal actions (e.g., funding a CCS project) must generally comply with NEPA, which often requires that an environmental assessment (EA) or environmental impact statement (EIS) be conducted to consider environmental impacts of the proposed action, including consideration of reasonable alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An EA determines whether or not a Federal action has the potential to cause significant environmental effects; agencies prepare an EIS if a proposed action is determined to significantly affect the quality of the human environment. The determination of the level of NEPA review depends on the potential for significant environmental impacts considering the whole project (e.g., crossings of sensitive habitats, cultural resources, wetlands, public safety concerns). Each Federal agency has adopted its own NEPA procedures for preparing EAs. If the agency determines the action will not have significant impacts it will issue a Finding of No Significant Impact (FONSI). Some projects may be categorically excluded. Procedural timing considerations (see separate metric) also apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEPA procedural deadlines (Fiscal Responsibility Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to NEPA in the Fiscal Responsibility Act established deadlines for the preparation of environmental assessments and environmental impact statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Environmental assessments must be completed within 1 year and environmental impact statements must be completed within 2 years. A lead agency that determines it is not able to meet the deadline may extend the deadline, in consultation with the applicant, to establish a new deadline that provides only so much additional time as is necessary to complete the EIS or EA.

rubrics_metrics.name: FAST-41 eligibility and use of the Permitting Dashboard
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fixing America's Surface Transportation Act (FAST-41) created procedures and funding authorities to improve Federal environmental review and authorization for covered infrastructure projects; the USE IT Act clarified that CCS projects and CO2 pipelines are eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FAST-41 created the Federal Permitting Improvement Steering Council and codified use of the Permitting Dashboard to track project timelines, including qualifying actions by EPA and other Federal agencies. Project sponsor participation in FAST-41 is voluntary; opting in can provide a more predictable and transparent review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of NETL CCS Pipeline Route Planning Database and siting tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Community engagement and routing decisions can be supported using the CCS Pipeline Route Planning Database developed by NETL, which is designed to support pipeline routing decisions and increase transportation safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The database includes state-specific regulations and restrictions, energy and social justice factors, land use requirements, existing infrastructure, and areas of potential risk. It produces weighted values from zero (acceptable areas) to one (areas to avoid). The database will be a key input for the NETL Pipeline Route Planning Tool under development to aid routing decisions and facilitate avoidance of areas that would pose permitting challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights-of-way acquisition and mitigation feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquisition of rights-of-way and easements for pipelines across various land types and ownership regimes has been routinely accomplished for many projects and can be feasible with appropriate mitigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited include thousands of miles of pipeline rights-of-way acquired across five states since 2021, the Citronelle Project obtaining rights across forested and wetland areas by mitigating environmental impacts, and interstate pipelines obtaining easements across state school trust lands, Federal land, and private land. The EPA notes many opportunities to reroute pipelines to minimize permitting challenges and landowner concerns; rights-of-way and permits can often be pursued simultaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: PHMSA regulatory standards for supercritical CO2 pipelines
rubrics_metrics.description: The safety of existing and new CO2 pipelines that transport CO2 in a supercritical state is regulated by PHMSA, which sets standards across multiple dimensions of pipeline safety and operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA regulations include standards related to pipeline design, pipeline construction and testing, pipeline operations and maintenance, operator reporting requirements, operator qualifications, corrosion control and pipeline integrity management, incident reporting and response, and public awareness and communications. PHMSA has authority to conduct inspections and issue notices for noncompliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-delegated authority and inspectorate responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain states have authority delegated from the U.S. Department of Transportation to conduct safety inspections and enforce state and Federal pipeline safety regulations for intrastate CO2 pipelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA's state partners employ about 70 percent of all pipeline inspectors, covering more than 80 percent of regulated pipelines. Federal law requires certified state authorities to adopt safety standards at least as stringent as Federal standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pipeline operator controls and required practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators must take required steps to ensure pipelines are operated safely under PHMSA and related state standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of required measures include the use of pressure monitors to detect leaks or initiate shut-off valves, annual reporting on operations, conducting structural integrity assessments, and performing inspections. These controls and standards are designed to ensure captured CO2 is securely conveyed to a sequestration site.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety record and incident data as part of adequacy assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical operational experience and incident statistics are used as evidence in assessing the safety of CO2 pipeline transport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EPA cites more than 60 years of CO2 pipeline operation, 500 million metric tons transported over 5,000 miles in the past 20 years with zero incidents involving fatalities, and PHMSA's report of 102 CO2 pipeline incidents between 2003 and 2022 with one injury and zero fatalities. Such data are used to support the conclusion that CO2 can be safely transported by pipeline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incident response and regulatory improvement following accidents
rubrics_metrics.description: PHMSA and other agencies respond to pipeline incidents with investigations, enforcement actions, advisories, and rulemaking to strengthen safety oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following the Satartia, Mississippi rupture, PHMSA initiated a rulemaking (NPRM submitted to OMB in Feb 2024), issued a Notice of Probable Violation/Proposed Civil Penalty/Proposed Compliance Order resolved by a Consent Agreement, issued updated nationwide advisory bulletins, and solicited research proposals to strengthen CO2 pipeline safety. Such responsive regulatory action is part of the safety assurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of proximity (100 km) as modeling proxy for pipeline complexity and cost
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA used a 100 km (62-mile) distance to the nearest potential sequestration site as an economic modeling assumption and proxy for pipeline complexity and transport costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 100 km assumption is based on NETL studies and is an economic modeling assumption (not meant to represent every EGU). EPA modeled unique distances for existing units and found 80 percent within 100 km and 11 percent within 160 km. For EGUs within 100 km, associated pipelines are expected to be shorter and more feasible; distance is a useful proxy for permitting complexity (e.g., interstate crossing, rights-of-way). EPA disagrees that 100 km is an inappropriate assumption given supporting studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: RULOF provisions for extending compliance schedules (40 CFR 60.2a(e)-(h))
rubrics_metrics.description: If a state can demonstrate that there is a fundamental difference between information relevant to a particular affected EGU and the information EPA considered in determining the compliance deadline, and that this difference makes it unreasonable for the EGU to meet the compliance deadline, a longer compliance schedule may be warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA states that the mere fact that a pipeline crosses state boundaries is not alone sufficient to show an extended timeframe is appropriate; rather, the confluence of factors (including interstate crossing along with other challenges) must be shown for RULOF to apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimated permitting timeline for pipelines relevant to compliance feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's anticipated permitting timeline for CO2 pipelines that only need an EA and for those requiring an EIS informs whether units can meet the compliance date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA anticipates the permitting process would take around 2.5 years for pipelines that only need an EA, with a possible additional year if the project requires an EIS. EPA uses this timeline in concluding that a compliance date of January 1, 2032 allows sufficient time for installations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geologic sequestration demonstration criteria (trapping and containment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Geologic sequestration is based on a demonstrated understanding of the trapping and containment processes that retain CO2 in the subsurface; the presence of a low permeability seal is an important component of demonstrating secure geologic sequestration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA references DOE and USGS analyses, NETL Atlas, and multiple demonstration projects showing that deep saline formations, unmineable coal seams, and oil and gas reservoirs can store CO2. Nearly every state has or is close to formations with sequestration potential; capacity estimates (DOE and USGS) indicate orders-of-magnitude more storage than needed under the rule. Demonstrations include DOE Regional Carbon Sequestration Partnerships, CarbonSAFE, and international projects (Sleipner, Snohvit, CarbFix).

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability and inventory analysis for sequestration sites relative to EGUs
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA performed a geographic availability analysis mapping areas with sequestration potential and distances from existing coal-fired steam generating capacity to potential sequestration sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: of the coal-fired capacity with planned operation after 2039, >50% is <32 km from potential deep saline sites, 73% <50 km, 80% <100 km, and 91% <160 km. At least 37 states have geologic characteristics amenable to deep saline sequestration; an additional 6 states are within 100 km of such formations. EPA uses these data to support assertions of broad availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: UIC Class VI regulatory framework and permitting practice as assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: The UIC Class VI program and the permitting process provide regulatory requirements intended to ensure the security of sequestered CO2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA and states with approved Class VI programs are reviewing Class VI permit applications; examples of permits issued (Wyoming, North Dakota, Louisiana, EPA-issued ADM permits in Decatur) and draft permits (Carbon TerraVault) illustrate the existence and functioning of the program. Conversions from Class II to Class VI wells are possible. The existence of active permitting, reviews, and issued permits supports that sequestration can be implemented under existing regulatory frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of EOR and unmineable coal seams as proven sequestration options
rubrics_metrics.description: Enhanced oil recovery (EOR) and enhanced coalbed methane recovery (in unmineable coal seams) are established practices that demonstrate CO2 injection and storage techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EOR has nearly 60 years of U.S. experience; unmineable coal seams have demonstrated pilot projects (e.g., Allison Unit) and DOE partnership projects. Technical considerations (e.g., coal swelling reducing injectivity) have available mitigation and design responses; existing infrastructure in depleted reservoirs can be evaluated for conversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project-scale demonstration and staged validation (DOE Regional Partnerships and CarbonSAFE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Field research projects and staged commercial-scale demonstration programs provide technical and managerial validation for geologic sequestration suitability and permitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE Regional Carbon Sequestration Partnerships injected over 12 million tons with no indications of negative health/environmental impacts. CarbonSAFE phases (I-III) involve feasibility, site characterization, risk assessment, CO2 management strategy development, and permitting to validate suitability for >50 million ton storage complexes. EPA cites ongoing projects, planned facilities, and injection well reviews as evidence of scalable demonstration.
